title: India's UPI Just Went Live in Greece. That's 10 Countries and Counting.
excerpt: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal witnessed the Eurobank-NPCI partnership launch in Athens, as India's digital payment system continues its quiet conquest of global finance.
body:
India's Unified Payments Interface has gone live in Greece, making it the tenth country where Indian travellers and residents can use the homegrown payment system for seamless digital transactions abroad.

Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who was in Athens for an official visit, witnessed the live demonstration of the Eurobank-NPCI International Payments Limited partnership at Eurobank's headquarters on Monday. The launch allows eligible customers to make instant, secure payments at reduced transaction costs compared to conventional cross-border transfer methods.

From the Eiffel Tower to the Parthenon

Greece joins an expanding list of countries that now accept UPI: Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka, and Cambodia. Each market supports varying levels of UPI integration — from merchant QR-code payments for tourists to full remittance corridors.

The European expansion has been particularly symbolic. UPI was launched at the Eiffel Tower in Paris in 2024, and more recently at Galeries Lafayette in Nice. Greece's Eurobank partnership, facilitated by Fairfax Digital Services, now brings UPI to the eastern Mediterranean — a region that sees significant Indian tourist traffic, particularly during the summer months.

"The increasing global acceptance and appreciation of UPI reflects the trust in India for building technology-led solutions that create value beyond borders," Goyal said in a post on X.

The Numbers Behind the Quiet Revolution

> ""The increasing global acceptance and appreciation of UPI reflects the trust in India for building technology-led solutions that create value beyond borders," Goyal said in a post on X."

The Greece launch comes on the heels of a blockbuster June for UPI domestically. According to data released by the National Payments Corporation of India on Wednesday, UPI processed 22.72 billion transactions worth ₹28.9 lakh crore ($344 billion) in June 2026 — a 20 percent year-on-year increase in value.

While the monthly total dipped slightly from May's record ₹29.9 lakh crore, the daily average hit an all-time high of 757 million transactions — more than the entire daily payment volume of many developed economies combined.

"These daily averages tell a very interesting story of how UPI has become the default mode of payment for low-value transactions," said Reeju Datta, co-founder of Cashfree Payments.

In just 12 months, UPI volumes have grown by over 4.3 billion transactions and nearly ₹5 lakh crore in value, underscoring how deeply embedded the system has become in India's economic infrastructure.

Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

For India's estimated 18.7 million-strong diaspora, UPI's international expansion has practical significance that goes beyond convenience at tourist spots.

The system is gradually being positioned as a low-cost remittance channel. India received over $100 billion in remittances in 2024 — the highest in the world — and reducing transaction costs on even a fraction of those flows represents billions in savings for families on both ends.

In countries where UPI is now live, Indian expatriates can transact using their international mobile numbers, bypassing the high banking fees and transfer delays that have long plagued cross-border money movement. As more remittance corridors integrate with UPI, the system could fundamentally alter how NRIs send money home.

The NPCI has signalled ambitions to expand to 30 more countries. If realised, this would position UPI not just as India's payment backbone but as a global digital payments standard — an outcome that Google's CEO Sundar Pichai acknowledged when he noted that Google Pay in India runs entirely on UPI rails.

What Makes UPI Different

UPI's international appeal lies partly in its architecture. Unlike card networks that charge merchants 2-3 percent per transaction, UPI operates on near-zero interchange fees domestically and dramatically reduced costs for cross-border payments. For small businesses in countries like Greece, accepting UPI from Indian tourists is essentially free revenue they would otherwise lose to cash or expensive card fees.

The system also represents a form of soft power. Every country that adopts UPI deepens its financial integration with India — and with the Reserve Bank of India's regulatory framework. It is, as one fintech analyst put it, "India exporting its financial infrastructure the way the US exported the dollar system."

What's Next

NPCI International Payments Limited is in discussions with banking partners in at least 20 more countries across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. The next wave of expansion is expected to focus on high-diaspora destinations: Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom — markets where Indian expatriates have long demanded cheaper, faster payment rails.

For now, Indian travellers heading to Athens this summer have one less reason to worry about currency exchange counters.
